claims.text: The as-deposited W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy has a single-phase BCC structure.
W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops Cr- and V-rich second-phase precipitates by approximately 8 dpa.
The irradiation-associated Cr-V-rich precipitates are approximately 3–5 nm in size.
Adding 3–5 at% Hf by replacing an equivalent amount of Cr and/or V will suppress Cr-V-rich precipitate formation up to about 8 dpa.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain the negligible irradiation hardening of the unmodified alloy.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain high radiation resistance.
A 3–5 at% Hf addition will remain compatible with practical bulk manufacture.
Hf will segregate to grain boundaries or triple junctions, or otherwise alter their local bonding environment.
Hf-induced changes in grain-boundary and triple-junction chemistry will reduce the mobility and clustering tendency of Cr and V.
Hf is a high-melting-point refractory element.
Hf increases lattice distortion and thereby modifies local defect dynamics and reduces solute diffusivity.
Reduced Cr and V mobility will hinder their co-segregation and suppress nucleation and growth of Cr-V-rich precipitates during irradiation.
The Hf-modified alloy will exhibit a statistically significant reduction in Cr-V-rich precipitate density relative to unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The Hf-modified alloy may exhibit smaller Cr-V-rich precipitates than the unmodified alloy.
Unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits near-negligible irradiation hardening after irradiation to 8 dpa.
Unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 shows no irradiation-created dislocation loops after irradiation to 8 dpa.
The baseline alloy was irradiated at room temperature and 1073 K to doses up to 8 dpa.
The beneficial Hf effect is expected to persist only up to approximately 8 dpa and 1073 K.
Increasing Hf substantially beyond 5 at% or exceeding 1073 K may eliminate the precipitation-suppression or manufacturability benefits.
Magnetron sputtering followed by consolidation is a practical bulk-manufacturable synthesis route for the proposed alloys.
